x: Visible light spans about 400–700 nm. 10–400 nm is ultraviolet, 0.01–10 nm is X-rays and 700 nm–1 mm is infrared.
t: Recall the EM spectrum bands in order of wavelength.

x: Microwave ovens use microwaves (about 2.45 GHz) that make water molecules vibrate and heat food. Infrared heats only surfaces.
t: Recall the use of each EM band.

x: Option C is incorrect: radio waves have the lowest frequency and longest wavelength in the spectrum; gamma rays have the highest frequency. The other uses are correct.
t: Recall the two ends of the EM spectrum.

x: Both are true and R explains A: photon energy is E = hν, and gamma rays have the highest frequency, so they carry the most energy.
t: Check whether R is the formula behind A.

x: A is true: X-rays are used in radiography and CT scans. R is false: cool stars and interstellar dust are studied with infrared, while X-ray astronomy studies hot gas and black holes.
t: Discriminate the astronomy use of each EM band.

x: X-rays are for radiography and CT, gamma rays for radiotherapy and PET, infrared for physiotherapy and thermal imaging, and microwaves for diathermy, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the medical use of each EM band.

x: Radio waves serve communication and radar, microwaves radar and jamming, infrared night vision and heat-seeking missiles, and gamma rays nuclear detection, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the defence use of each EM band.

x: I and II are correct: radio waves carry radio, TV and mobile signals, and microwaves serve satellites, radar and 5G. III is false because UV, X-rays and gamma rays are ionising and not used for normal communication.
t: Discriminate communication bands from ionising bands.

x: In increasing wavelength the order is gamma rays, visible light, infrared, radio waves, giving B, D, A, C.
t: Recall the spectrum order: gamma, X, UV, visible, IR, micro, radio.

x: Three are infrared defence uses: night vision, heat-seeking missiles and surveillance. Baggage and cargo scanning uses X-rays.
t: Discriminate infrared uses from X-ray uses.

x: Gamma rays are below 0.01 nm, X-rays 0.01–10 nm, UV 10–400 nm, IR 700 nm–1 mm, microwaves 1 mm–1 m and radio waves above 1 m, giving a-iii, b-vi, c-v, d-i, e-iv, f-ii.
t: Recall the wavelength boundaries of each band.

x: All six are correct: the frequency ranges rise from radio through microwave, infrared, visible and ultraviolet to X-rays, each matching c = fλ.
t: Recall that frequency rises as wavelength falls.

x: Energy rises with frequency: radio waves are lowest, then microwaves (lower), infrared (low), visible (medium), ultraviolet (high) and X-rays (very high), giving a-v, b-ii, c-iv, d-vi, e-iii, f-i.
t: Recall E = hν to rank energy.

x: All three are radio-wave uses: cellular networks, radar ranging, and Wi-Fi and Bluetooth for short-range wireless links.
t: Recall the uses of radio waves.

x: Microwave radar is used in speed guns, weather radar and aircraft detection. Radiotherapy uses gamma rays and remotes use infrared.
t: Recall the use of each EM band.

x: Both are true and say the same thing: microwave satellite links use an uplink from Earth and a downlink back.
t: Check whether the two statements are just restatements.

x: Wi-Fi works in the 2.4 and 5 GHz microwave bands, at the high-frequency end of the radio region.
t: Recall the frequency band used by Wi-Fi.

x: Microwave links give point-to-point communication, remotes use infrared, thermal cameras give night vision and IR heaters give heating, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the uses of microwaves and infrared.

x: Both are true: infrared satellites map clouds and temperature for weather forecasts, and motion sensors and night cameras use infrared for security.
t: Recall the uses of infrared.

x: Some infrared wavelengths, near 1.3–1.55 μm, carry signals in fibre optics. The other options use "only" or "not", which are false.
t: Check each option for the words "only" and "not".

x: Visible light lets us see, cameras use it for photography, some visible wavelengths are used in optical fibres, and lasers serve pointers, surgery and industry, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the uses of visible light.

x: All three are visible-light uses: LEDs and bulbs for lighting, spectroscopy for analysis, and screens for display.
t: Recall the uses of visible light.

x: All five are UV uses: sterilising lamps, water purifiers, forgery-detection markers, vitamin D synthesis in skin and fluorescence in forensics.
t: Recall the uses of ultraviolet.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: sunburn and skin cancer are harmful effects of UV, not why UV is used to study hot stars.
t: Check whether R is a reason or a side fact.

x: Photolithography uses ultraviolet light, including deep and extreme UV, to print fine circuit patterns on silicon chips.
t: Recall the industrial use of ultraviolet.

x: Radiographs image bones and the chest, CT scans give detailed body images, and airport X-rays scan baggage, giving a-iii, b-i, c-ii.
t: Recall the uses of X-rays.

x: X-ray crystallography finds crystal and DNA structure, industrial X-rays find cracks, X-ray astronomy studies hot gas and black holes, and high-energy X-rays treat cancer, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Recall the uses of X-rays.

x: All four are gamma-ray uses: killing cancer cells, sterilising instruments and food, PET and gamma-camera imaging, and industrial thickness gauging and weld inspection.
t: Recall the uses of gamma rays.

x: All three are correct: gamma-ray astronomy studies bursts and neutron stars, nuclear medicine uses gamma-emitting tracers, and gamma detectors find nuclear materials.
t: Recall the uses of gamma rays.

x: Both are true: UV is used for sterilisation, vitamin D and skin treatment, and visible light for laser surgery, endoscopy and illumination.
t: Recall the medical uses of each EM band.

x: MRI uses radio-frequency pulses, infrared runs remotes and short-range data links, and visible light is used in Li-Fi and some fibres, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i.
t: Recall the use of each EM band.

x: Visible and infrared lasers are used for range finding, targeting and directed-energy weapons. Crystallography and CT use X-rays, and PET uses gamma rays.
t: Recall the defence uses of lasers.

x: Radio telescopes study pulsars and the CMB, microwave astronomy studies the CMB, optical telescopes study stars and galaxies, and UV astronomy studies hot young stars, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the target of each type of astronomy.

x: X-ray astronomy studies black holes, neutron stars and hot gas in galaxy clusters. Cool stars and dust are infrared targets, and gamma-ray bursts are gamma targets.
t: Recall the target of each type of astronomy.

x: 4G and 5G mobile networks use microwave frequencies. AM/FM uses lower radio frequencies and remotes use infrared.
t: Recall the use of each EM band.

x: Infrared astronomy sees cool stars and interstellar dust. Black holes are X-ray targets, gamma-ray bursts are gamma targets and hot young stars are UV targets.
t: Match each type of astronomy to the temperature of its target.
